item.title: Application of AI in Conducting Numerical Experiments and Preparing Papers for Exploratory Research
item.description:
Hello everyone. My name is Maxim Shevchenko. I've worked as a manual tester (among other things); I consider myself a researcher, primarily in the field of mathematics. In this publication, I want to share my personal experience and results using the LLM Gemini in conjunction with Python for conducting numerical experiments and preparing papers for my mathematical research. This research is exploratory in nature. There's no rigid plan here; the methodology is more akin to Agile than Waterfall. In my collaboration with AI, I encountered both its advantages and disadvantages, which I'd like to share. Read more

item.title: Why AI Models Need to Self-Replicate. Or is it Not Them Who Need It?
item.description:
In a recent Anthropic article, researchers explored how lightweight open-weight models can copy themselves onto compromised consumer and IoT devices and run local inference. The researchers claim they can, but I believe there's no economic sense in it. In this article, I examine what AI proliferation truly means and how it will likely look in reality. Read more

item.title: Accelerating Wine Development with AI
item.description:
Hello, Habr! This is Ivan Sorokin, you know me from articles about far2l, its ideological successor f4, and the port of Dos Navigator to modern systems. I want to tell you about a new project (actually, projects) that you will surely like and find useful! Introducing fix-it-in-wine and dllmgr. The first is a skill that allows you to assign an AI agent the task of fixing compatibility errors of Windows applications with Wine. The second is something like a package manager for DLLs: it allows you to install fixed libraries independently of the main Wine, share them, and use ready-made solutions from other developers. But the main idea here is not even to teach AI to fix Wine errors. It is to change the very model of development and distribution of fixes. Read more

item.title: [Translation] Claude Code unbiased
item.description:
I once asked Claude Code which CMS it would recommend. I wanted to see where it was leaning. It answered: Drupal. No way. I asked why, and it explained that it saw my custom Drupal skill and decided that I work with Drupal and would be comfortable with it. Fair enough. My instructions, skills, and settings make the agent biased. But for this question, I needed an unbiased one. A regular chatbot would have sufficed, but we don't take the easy way, do we? 😁 I started looking for how to run Claude Code without my own config and found the --safe-mode flag. According to the description, it's just what I needed: no CLAUDE.md, skills, plugins, hooks, or MCP servers, and my subscription as usual. Pure default Claude Code ✨ I asked again. Drupal again. (╯°□°)╯︵ ┻━┻ This time the path was as follows: my email in the agent's context → amazee.io domain → a company known for Drupal hosting → the user works in a Drupal-oriented company. So much for pure Claude Code. Read more

item.title: AI Agent Context: What to Store, What to Read, and What to Trust
item.description:
Following my move from Claude Code to Codex on Habr, a debate arose: is dialogue history needed if Git, documentation, and specifications exist? I examined arguments, tools, and research. It turns out the problem is much broader. In early November, I wrote on Habr about how, after the paid Claude Code organization was blocked, I switched to Codex and tried to preserve project history. The code remained on my computer, the repositories didn't disappear. But over several months, dozens of conversations about architecture, bugs, experiments, and plans accumulated. Not everything made it into the documentation. The built-in import in Codex proved inconvenient: out of 25 projects and 53 chats, about 50 sessions were transferred, but linking conversations to projects was unsuccessful. Eventually, I found Hansard and started accessing old history through search. I thought that would be the end of the story. However, a debate began in the comments. Read more

item.title: How to Set Up AI Agents in OpenCode with Your Own Provider
item.description:
If you're up-to-date with the news of the last three years, you've surely heard of the term AI agent. You might have even used or known about AI agent systems like Claude Code or Codex. Initially, they might seem like marketing hype to justify the AI bubble – why build an abstract structure, pay for tokens, and configure agents and sub-agents when you can just use a standard AI chat interface: open the chat, paste text, formulate a prompt, and get output. Does it simplify our lives? Absolutely! But it quickly hits a ceiling. A model is just a model; it doesn't know the context or work directly with your project. An AI agent, however, is a whole system, not just an LLM but an LLM + harness. The problem is, Claude Code and Codex are closed-source, proprietary, and only for their models. This is where OpenCode comes in – an open-source harness system where an agent model can read files, run tests, call other models, delegate work to sub-agents, and connect MCPs, skills, and plugins. Most importantly, it's not tied to a single vendor. You can use official or third-party providers and call any available models, from GLM 5.3 to Claude Opus 5.5. In this article, I'll cover the basics of creating AI agents in OpenCode by connecting an OpenAI-compatible gateway. Read on

item.title: 8 Interesting Ways to Use GPT-6 Astra That Not Everyone Knows About
item.description:
People use Astra to create 3D games, animations, product ads, and interactive paintings. In the article, I will share examples of use that I liked. Many people who use GPT-6 Astra actively share their experiments on X and Reddit. There are plenty of familiar ways to use it, but some are hard to ignore. Someone makes the neural network draw portraits in good old Paint, someone uses it to create motion graphics in After Effects, and someone brings paintings to life, turning them into explorable spaces. I have selected eight projects that I liked the most, and for each, I have added a couple of my thoughts on where such an approach could be useful. Replicating them is not difficult: you need access to Astra and the program the author used. Read more

item.title: Can System Prompts Be Replaced by Initial State? Experiments on RWKV-7
item.description:
What is the initial state of a model? Why can RWKV's initial state replace a system prompt? And how does it differ from a regular prompt? Answers to these questions in this article. A regular transformer reads the system prompt anew with each request and stores it in a cache that grows with the text. RWKV is structured differently: after reading any text, it compresses everything it remembers into a fixed-size 'memory', i.e., a state. This state is empty before starting work, meaning it can be non-empty. There are two ways: read the prompt once and save the resulting state (I call this 'folding' the prompt), or find a state through training without touching the model's weights. In both cases, the prompt text is no longer needed. I tested both methods on RWKV-7 models from 0.4B to 2.9B parameters on a regular MacBook M4 16GB. Everything was computed in SwiftRWKV, and quantized bases were made in rwkv-quant (described in my previous article RWKV-7 Quantization: What Breaks in Models of Different Sizes). Below: what I found, where it works better than a text prompt, and where it breaks. Verdict. Yes - for an unchanging instruction on models of this size, if the state is trained on filtered data. The gain is in speed, sometimes in accuracy and stability; the state does not add knowledge. Details and limitations - below. In short: Folded prompt - a free and accurate cache. It gives the same answers as the prompt text, and for long prompts, the request starts up to 13 times faster. Prompt in a string can degrade the model. On questions with verifiable answers, it reduced accuracy by 3-15 points on all eight tested models. A trained state was never significantly worse than a model without a prompt and always better than a prompt. The state learns the form of the answer, not new knowledge - and it needs filtered data. If it copies the teacher's mistakes, the state inherits them. The state is no worse than LoRA on the same data: half the parameters, weights are not changed. Compared to fine-tuning the upper layers in generation, it is better or no worse (in the embedder - no). Weaknesses: leading questions ('Are you Claude?') and long dialogues. Both can be improved - with caveats below. It also works where the model does not follow the instruction from the text at all: 0.4B classifies news with a prompt at 0.00, with a trained state - at 0.84–0.89. Each point below has a graph and a link to full tables. Read more

item.title: Vibe coding vs. a hundred shards: how I built Terox in a couple of days
item.description:
When a service runs on a hundred PostgreSQL shards, even the question "where is the record with this ID located?" can easily turn into iterating through dozens of connections. Entities are distributed using consistent hashing, and rare operations on heavily loaded tables require careful monitoring of lock_timeout, statement_timeout, and connection pools. I'm a backend developer for high-load services, formerly a DBA. Our standard migrations are rolled out automatically. But when a change requires special control on a heavily loaded table, I don't want to rely solely on the developer having checked the script and not forgotten anything. Thus, after a couple of days of collaboration with AI, Terox was created – a CLI that searches for data across a set of shards, switches to the found one, and rolls out complex SQL via dry-run, canary, and batches. I'll explain how a work pain turned into an open-source tool and why, when working with production databases, vibe coding quickly turns into regular engineering work. Taming a hundred shards
